pedagogy.summary: Children compare how much containers HOLD (capacity) using the language full/empty/half full/more than/less than, and by POURING from one container to another. The central hurdle is conservation of liquid: don't judge the amount by the height of the liquid or the tallness of the container — a tall thin glass can hold less than a short wide one, and the same amount looks different in different-shaped containers. Compare by pouring into a common container.
bestPractices: Compare by POURING — pour one container into the other, or both into identical bottles — rather than eyeballing liquid levels
Deliberately contrast a tall-thin container with a short-wide one so height is repeatedly misleading
Use full / empty / half full / quarter full and more/less language in context
Make it practical: water and sand play with real containers
Name the key idea: the same amount can look different in different containers
commonMisconceptions: Taller liquid level or taller container = more (height-vs-amount / conservation of liquid)
Wider or physically bigger container = more, judging the container not the contents
Thinks pouring the same water into a different-shaped container changes the amount
Guesses from appearance instead of pouring to test

learn.summary: Young children (ages 4-6) compare how much containers HOLD (capacity) using the language full / empty / half full / quarter full / more than / less than, and by POURING water or sand from one container to another. The core hurdle is conservation of liquid: children tend to judge amount by the height of the liquid or the size of the container rather than by what it actually holds. The reliable strategy is to pour into a common container (or pour one into the other) to test, repeatedly contrasting a tall-thin container with a short-wide one so that height stops being trusted.

activities.title: Pour the same water back and forth (conservation)
feedback: If the child says the tall glass has more 'because the water is higher', invite them to pour both into identical beakers and watch the levels come out about the same: the amount didn't change with the shape.
Repeat with fresh tall-thin vs short-wide pairs until the child stops trusting height and reaches for the pour-and-compare check.
When a child predicts before pouring and then checks, name the strategy: 'You poured to test instead of guessing from how it looks.'
activities.rationale: Conservation is revealed by holding the quantity fixed while changing the container shape: pouring the same water between a tall-thin and a short-wide container, then into matching beakers, lets the child see the level change while the amount stays the same. An optional live amount readout (e.g. a 'ml held' counter that stays constant while the level jumps) can make the invariance explicit, but the pouring itself is the mechanism, not the readout.
sourceClaims: NCETM Year 1 uses a Captain Conjecture prompt on conservation of liquid — 'All of the glasses contain the same quantity of lemonade. Do you agree? Explain' (glasses of differing width/height with liquid at the same level) — and pouring tasks (pour a 1-litre bottle into a 2-litre bottle and mark the level; bottle vs jug capacity; half-as-full / twice-as-full), directly probing whether children confuse height with amount.
learnerActions: Fill a tall thin glass with water and set an empty short wide bowl beside it, ready to pour the same water from one to the other.
Pour the water from the tall glass into the empty wide bowl and back again; notice the level is high in the glass and low in the bowl, even though it is the same water.

Predict first, then pour each of two mystery containers (secretly holding the same amount) into its own identical beaker and check: the levels come out about the same (small spills or drips can make a tiny difference).
Say aloud what happened: the tall one never had more, it just looked that way because the glass is thin.
Hit half-full and quarter-full targets by pouring until the water reaches a marked line (about half, about a quarter is fine at this age).
activities.intendedInsight: The same amount of water can look very different in differently-shaped containers; when the containers are different shapes, the height of the liquid (or the tallness of the container) does not by itself tell you the amount. To be sure, pour into identical containers, where comparing the levels is fair.

activities.title: Which holds more? Compare capacity by pouring into a common measure
feedback: If the child picks the physically bigger or wider container regardless of the pour, pour both into matching bottles and show the result; set up a narrow-tall container that holds more than a wide-short one so size alone is misleading.
If the child pours a full cup into the jug and the jug isn't filled, help them say 'the jug holds more because one cupful doesn't fill it.'
Prompt 'how could you check?' and model pouring into a common container when the child guesses from appearance.
activities.rationale: Measurement at this stage is comparison through a practical activity; using a shared container greater than the things being compared (filling each and pouring into matching bottles) gives a fair comparison and counters judging by container size. A deliberately counter-intuitive narrow-tall-holds-more case keeps the 'bigger-looking = more' misconception in check.
sourceClaims: Standard units can be introduced through a unit greater than the things being compared — e.g. comparing the capacity of a cup and a carton by filling each and pouring into matching bottles to compare; measurement is comparison and a practical activity.

Year 1 pupils compare, describe and solve practical problems for capacity and volume [full/empty, more than, less than, half, half full, quarter] and 'measure and begin to record' capacity and volume; at this stage volume and capacity are used interchangeably.
learnerActions: Take two containers that look different in size — e.g. a cup and a jug, or a wide-short container and a narrow-tall one.
Fill each and pour into matching identical bottles/beakers so you can compare fairly by what each holds.
Decide which holds more by looking at the common bottles, not at the original containers.
Try a deliberately tricky case: a narrow-tall container that actually holds MORE than a wide-short one.
activities.intendedInsight: Capacity is about how much a container holds, which you find by pouring and comparing in a common measure — not by how big or wide the container looks.

activities.title: Real water and sand play with the language
feedback: When a child names a level, check it together: in a straight-sided container, does 'half full' really reach about the middle? (In a bowl or a container that narrows or widens, half the height is not half the amount.) Let them adjust by pouring.
If a child compares by eyeballing, encourage pouring one into the other to settle it.
Celebrate correct use of full/empty/half-full/quarter-full/more/less in running commentary rather than only at the end.
activities.rationale: Comparing capacity is inherently practical; the Year 1 curriculum frames measurement as comparison and a practical activity. Real water and sand play with physical containers gives the hands-on pouring experience and naturalises the full/empty/half/quarter and more/less vocabulary in context, making it a core practical experience for this age alongside any screen model.
sourceClaims: Year 1 pupils compare, describe and solve practical problems for capacity and volume [full/empty, more than, less than, half, half full, quarter] and 'measure and begin to record' capacity and volume; at this stage volume and capacity are used interchangeably.

Standard units can be introduced through a unit greater than the things being compared — e.g. comparing the capacity of a cup and a carton by filling each and pouring into matching bottles to compare; measurement is comparison and a practical activity.
learnerActions: At a water or sand tray, fill, empty and pour between real containers of different shapes and sizes.
Describe containers as full, empty, half full and quarter full as you fill them.
Compare two containers aloud using 'more than' and 'less than'.
Make a glass that is 'about half full' and another that is 'about quarter full'.
Solve a practical problem such as 'Which cup has more water?' by pouring to find out.
activities.intendedInsight: Capacity language and comparison are grounded in the practical, hands-on act of filling, emptying and pouring with real materials.

activities.title: Scored comparison and fill-level items (check, not discovery)
feedback: For a wrong 'holds more' choice, return to real or simulated pouring into a common container to resolve it.
For a mismatched fill label, show the container and ask the child to point to where half or quarter would be.
Treat these items as a check on understanding, not as the place where the conservation idea is first built — these items do not let the child perform the pour-to-test action themselves.
activities.rationale: Comparison and fill-level language make clean scored items that assess recognition and application. These items check understanding but do not let the child pour to test, so independent construction of the conservation strategy should be built first in the pouring activities. Recognition alone does not elicit the child's own pour-to-test production.
learnerActions: From pictures of pour outcomes, choose which container holds more.
Match containers to the labels full, half full and empty.
Put a set of containers in order by how much they hold.
Explain, where asked, how you could check an answer by pouring.
activities.intendedInsight: Children can recognise and apply capacity and fill-level language and reason about which holds more from pour evidence.

constraints: Compare by POURING — pour one container into the other, or both into identical bottles/beakers — rather than eyeballing liquid levels.
Deliberately and repeatedly contrast a tall-thin container with a short-wide one so height is shown to be misleading more than once.
Use full / empty / half full / quarter full and more than / less than in context, not as isolated vocabulary drills.
At this stage volume and capacity are used interchangeably (per Year 1 curriculum notes).
A static tall-thin/short-wide pair with a 'same amount!' reveal can name the idea but does not let the child test it by pouring; use it to introduce or summarise, not as the only experience.
Recognition/scored items assess and reinforce but do not elicit the child's own pour-to-test action; pair them with hands-on or interactive pouring.
An optional constant 'amount held' readout alongside a changing level can make invariance explicit, but it is one way to show the idea, not a required mechanism.
Tilt-and-pour 3D models and 2D pouring sims offer different experiences; neither is required, and real water/sand play remains the natural companion for this age.
Half/quarter full targets are approximate at this age ('about half full'); exact fractional precision is not expected.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The legacy source claimed a 2D pouring sim is preferable because 'capacity is about quantity, not spatial form', that a tilt-and-pour 3D version 'adds nothing but overhead', and that 'dialogue cannot supply the pouring.' These are catalog-fit preferences, not established comparative-efficacy findings; they have been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements. 3D and dialogue can still support learning in other ways.

The claim that a static image 'cannot let the child test it by pouring' is a genuine objective limit (no manipulation of a fixed picture) and is retained as scoped; it is not asserted that a static image 'cannot teach' the idea.
Half-full / quarter-full targets are approximate for this age ('about half full'); exact fractional precision is not expected.

The scored-items activity has sourceClaims [] because no cited source directly supports its recognition/assessment rationale; the recognition-vs-production limit is stated as an objective affordance, not as a sourced effectiveness finding.

The National Curriculum Year 1 claim is topic/coverage-level support; it was removed from the conservation activity (which it does not address) and retained only where the comparison and full/half/quarter vocabulary it lists is directly used.

The conservation activity narrative uses two mystery containers each holding the same amount, poured into separate identical beakers; the 'pour back and forth' step is a demonstrative lead-in and the subsequent prediction step uses a fresh equal-amount pair.

probeDeeper: 'The water looks higher in this glass — does higher always mean more? How could you be sure?'
'If I pour the tall glass's water into this wide bowl, will there be more, less, or the same water? Why?' (conservation, fresh case)
'What does “half full” mean — can you show me on this glass?'
assess.correctAnswer: (1) Recognises you can't tell from the levels alone and pours into identical beakers (or one into the other) to compare — finding them equal. (2) Determines capacity by pouring (the jug holds more because the cupful doesn't fill it). (3) Identifies or makes a half-full glass. Uses full / half full / more / less correctly.

errorPatterns.pattern: Height = amount — the taller liquid level (or taller glass) must have more, judged without pouring
errorPatterns.nextMove: Pour both into identical beakers so the levels match — the amount didn't change with the shape; repeat with tall-thin vs short-wide until height stops being trusted.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task 1 says the tall thin glass has more 'because the water is higher', declining to pour

errorPatterns.pattern: Bigger / wider container = more — judges the container rather than what it holds
errorPatterns.nextMove: Pour to test capacity directly; contrast a wide-short container with a narrow-tall one that actually holds more.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On task 2 picks the physically bigger container as holding more regardless of the actual pour

errorPatterns.pattern: Guesses from looking instead of pouring to test when pouring is available
errorPatterns.nextMove: Prompt 'how could you check?' and model pouring into a common container — a strategy prompt, not a reteach.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives an answer without using the pour-and-compare strategy

responseLevels.gap: Judges amount by the height of the liquid or the size of the container; doesn't think to pour.
responseLevels.full: Compares capacity by pouring into a common container, is not fooled by container shape or liquid height, and recognises the amount is conserved when the same water is poured into a differently-shaped container.
responseLevels.partial: Uses full/empty/half-full language and compares obvious cases, but is fooled by tall-thin vs short-wide (says taller = more) unless prompted to pour.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Set out a tall thin glass and a short wide glass holding the SAME amount of water (so the levels differ), a cup, a jug, and some empty identical beakers. Watch how the child decides: (1) 'Do these two glasses have the same amount of water, or does one have more? How could you find out?' (2) 'Pour this full cup into the jug — which holds more, the cup or the jug?' (3) 'Show me a glass that is about half full.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The equal-amount-different-height pair is the classic conservation probe — a child fooled by height says the tall glass has more; a child who conserves says 'pour them together to check'. Item 2 catches whether they compare by what a container holds (pouring) rather than by how big it looks.
